asr.full_text: Hello? When Jacob de Lys picked up the phone the other day he knew he had a problem. I was pretty suspicious right from the beginning. So de Lys recorded the conversation. On the line, a man claiming to be from Microsoft. He wanted to get onto my computer to show me how badly corrupted it was and that he would fix it from there. Those who fall for it are conned into paying a fee for having their computer cleaned or they give scammers access to their computer allowing spyware to be installed. According to Microsoft every year more than 2.8 million Canadians get a tech scam call. Of those, 200,000 lose money to the scam and it is a lot of money, more than $347 million dollars a year. Canadian anti-fraud centre, how may I help you? 80% of calls to Canada's anti-fraud centre are now about this one ripoff. And now they're claiming even more victims online. The bad guys are setting up their own websites, making it seem like they are connected with Microsoft or whoever else. The scammers are clearly getting more aggressive just ask Deleese, he called the scammer a thief and a bad person for trying to rip people off. We have our group, our group in Canada. Ok I will call them, I will provide the information to them- they will come to you and they will kill you. Oh, so you're threatening to kill me? Would you like that? No? He was still trying to get me to do what I was what he was telling me to do with my computer So it's the scam that neither Microsoft nor police can seem to get a handle on Microsoft repeating the message. It's been trying to get out there. It never calls customers to charge for computer fixes. The company also tells Go Pubblic it's now sharing information about Canadian victims with Canadian authorities. But as far as we can tell, no action against the scammers has been taken by the company or by police on behalf of victims in this country. Rosa Marcatelli, CBC News, Calgary. textual.observation: A caller claiming to be from Microsoft sought access to the viewer's computer while offering to show that it was corrupted and fix it; the report states that people who comply may be charged a cleaning fee or allow computer access for spyware installation.

evidence.quote: On the line, a man claiming to be from Microsoft. He wanted to get onto my computer to show me how badly corrupted it was and that he would fix it from there.
Those who fall for it are conned into paying a fee for having their computer cleaned or they give scammers access to their computer allowing spyware to be installed.

textual.context: Presented in a news report and warning about alleged tech-support scam calls, not as an endorsement of the caller's request.
textual.potential_relevance: The claimed Microsoft affiliation and promised computer repair are linked to a request for computer access and a possible cleaning fee, with the report also describing a stated spyware-installation mechanism.
textual.limitations: These records do not independently verify the caller's identity, the alleged software installation, any payment, or the reported outcomes.

textual.observation: The report describes people setting up websites that appear connected to Microsoft or another company while seeking to reach potential victims online.

evidence.quote: The bad guys are setting up their own websites, making it seem like they are connected with Microsoft or whoever else.

textual.context: The website statement is attributed to a news report describing alleged scam activity; the description separately directs viewers to a CBC news story.
textual.potential_relevance: A purported affiliation with Microsoft or another company is linked to websites used to reach potential victims, which may require assessment of the destination and identity claim.
textual.limitations: The supplied records do not identify a specific scam website, show its contents, or establish that the CBC link is one of the websites described.

visual.observation: An on-screen news graphic states that a recorded caller described as a tech-support scammer threatened a British Columbia man, and the accompanying image shows a phone-call scene with the displayed threat, "They will come to you, they will kill you."
visual.context: The material is presented in a news-reporting context; frame F0064 shows a CBC News page headline describing the recorded call.
visual.potential_relevance: The visible relationship between a reported tech-support scam call and a threatening statement provides a concretely described scam-related mechanism and coercive communication for review.
visual.limitations: The sampled frames do not establish who made the call, whether the displayed threat is verbatim, whether the caller was actually a scammer, or what actions or information the recipient was asked to provide.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is CBC news coverage warning viewers about people pretending to be from Microsoft. It reports a caller's alleged request for computer access and possible repair payment, along with a reported threat, while showing a CBC reporter and an anti-fraud-centre representative. The reported requests are presented as part of the incident being covered, not as an offer from the video creator or a solicitation to the audience.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary subject is a warning and investigation of a reported third-party tech-support scam, including a claimed Microsoft identity, a computer-access request and an alleged threat. The supplied material presents these actions as the incident being reported, not as an offer or solicitation by the video creator.
